subject: Biology
title: Brain-Computer Interfaces
description: A quick, practical guide to Brain-Computer Interfaces.

hook.text: Imagine controlling a computer or robotic arm with nothing but your thoughts.

buildup.text: Brain-computer interfaces read electrical signals from neurons and translate them into commands.

discovery.text: Paralyzed patients have used implants to type, move cursors, and even control robotic limbs.

twist.text: Neuralink and similar companies aim to implant chips in healthy brains to enhance cognition.

climax.text: The technology raises deep questions about privacy, identity, and what it means to be human.

punchline.text: Thoughts become commands. The interface is the brain.

quiz.question: What have paralyzed patients achieved using brain-computer interfaces?

details.summary: Brain-computer interfaces connect neural activity directly to external devices, allowing paralyzed patients to control cursors, robotic arms, or communication software using only their thoughts. Electrodes detect neural firing patterns that software translates into commands.
details.whyItMatters: BCIs offer hope for people with paralysis, locked-in syndrome, and neurodegenerative diseases. They represent a frontier where neuroscience meets engineering to restore lost communication and movement.
takeaways: Electrodes detect neural signals and translate them into device commands
Invasive BCIs offer higher precision but require brain surgery
Non-invasive BCIs use EEG but with lower signal resolution

faq.question: How does a brain-computer interface actually work?
faq.answer: Electrodes implanted in or placed on the brain detect electrical patterns from neurons firing. Machine learning algorithms decode these patterns into intended actions like moving a cursor left or gripping with a robotic hand.

faq.question: Are brain-computer interfaces safe for long-term use?
faq.answer: Invasive BCIs carry risks of infection, immune response, and signal degradation as scar tissue forms around electrodes. Research is improving biocompatible materials and wireless designs to make long-term implants safer and more reliable.
